captions.text: on Wall Street. The smartest guys in the room.
Exactly. They built these massively heavily leveraged portfolios
based on complex Gaussian copular models.
Their models looked at decades of historical data and
assumed that nationwide home prices could never decline all
at once across the entire country.
Right. They equated historical price stability with future
safety. Exactly. They looked at their neat historical models
and relied on normal outcomes prevailing.
They literally engineered their portfolios.
assuing a nationwide housing crash, a true black swan
outlier, was a statistical which
is wild in hindsight.
And because they thought risk was gone, they leveraged
up 30 to1. So when reality
broke their models, they were utterly decimated.
They confused the map for the territory.
Joel Greenblat actually chimes in on this exact point
in the text, pointing out that many academic versions
of risk completely miss the practical reality
of investing. Give us an example.
Let's say a company's stock price drops by 50%
in a week because of a broad market panic,
but the underlying business is incredibly sound.
It has zero debt and it's generating massive free
cash flow. According to academic models, the
stock's beta or volatility has just skyrocketed,
meaning the stock is now quote unquote riskier because
[clears throat] the price moves so much, right?
